howItWorks.intro: Stamp duty (officially "transfer duty" in NSW, Victoria, Queensland and WA) isn't a flat percentage of what you pay for a property. Every state and territory runs its own progressive bracket system, much like income tax: the first slice of the purchase price is taxed at a low rate, the next slice at a higher rate, and so on up the ladder, with only the portion of the price that falls inside each bracket taxed at that bracket's rate. Because NSW, VIC, QLD, WA, SA, TAS, ACT and the NT each set their own thresholds and rates — and revise them in most state budgets — the same $600,000 house can attract noticeably different duty depending on which side of a border it sits on. This calculator applies the bracket structure for the state or territory you select, then layers on any first home buyer concession and foreign purchaser surcharge that apply.
rules: Stamp duty is calculated on progressive bands that vary by state/territory
First home buyer exemptions vary by state (e.g., NSW up to $800k, VIC up to $600k)
Foreign buyer surcharges: 7-8% additional on top of standard duty
howItWorks.outro: Treat every figure here as a planning estimate, not a settlement figure. State treasuries adjust duty thresholds, rates, first home buyer caps and foreign purchaser surcharges on their own schedules — sometimes mid-financial-year — so a bracket table that's accurate today can be superseded by the next state budget. Before you exchange contracts, confirm the exact amount payable with your state or territory revenue office (Revenue NSW, the State Revenue Office in Victoria, Queensland Revenue Office, and so on) or ask your conveyancer or solicitor to run the calculation as part of your contract review. They'll also catch concessions tied to your specific contract date, land use, or residency status that a generic calculator can't see.

faq.question: How is stamp duty actually calculated in Australia?
faq.answer: Duty isn't a single percentage applied to the whole price — it's worked out bracket by bracket, the same way income tax brackets work. Each state publishes a table of price bands and a rate for each band, and only the portion of the price sitting inside a given band is taxed at that band's rate. A $650,000 purchase in NSW, for example, pays a low rate on the first $17,000, a slightly higher rate on the next $19,000, and so on up through the bands until you reach the band the full price falls into. That's why effective duty on, say, a $400,000 unit is a much smaller share of the price than duty on a $2 million house — the higher bands only bite on the dollars above each threshold, not on the whole purchase.

faq.question: Can you show a worked example of the bracket calculation?
faq.answer: Using NSW's general (non-first-home-buyer) duty bands on a $650,000 established home: 1.25% on the first $17,000 = $212.50; 1.5% on the next $19,000 (to $36,000) = $285.00; 1.75% on the next $61,000 (to $97,000) = $1,067.50; 3.5% on the next $267,000 (to $364,000) = $9,345.00; then 4.5% on the remaining $286,000 up to $650,000 = $12,870.00. Add those five slices together and you land on roughly $23,780 in transfer duty — around 3.7% of the purchase price, not a flat rate. Change the state, the price, or the buyer's first-home or foreign-purchaser status and every one of those numbers moves, which is exactly what this calculator recalculates for you.

faq.question: Do first home buyers get a stamp duty exemption or concession?
faq.answer: In most states, yes, but the cut-offs and the mechanism differ. NSW has historically waived duty entirely below one threshold and phased in a reduced rate up to a second, higher threshold; Victoria exempts eligible first home buyers below one price point and tapers a concession up to a higher one; Queensland, SA, WA, Tasmania, the ACT and NT each run their own version with their own caps. Eligibility usually also depends on whether the property is new or established, whether you'll live in it, and whether you or your co-buyer have owned residential property before anywhere in Australia. Because these thresholds move with each state budget, treat any number you see — including in this calculator — as indicative and verify the current cap with your state revenue office before relying on it.

faq.question: Is there a surcharge for foreign purchasers?
faq.answer: Yes. Every state and territory that charges transfer duty also charges an additional foreign purchaser (or "foreign buyer") surcharge on top of the standard duty, typically landing somewhere in the 7–8% range of the property value depending on the state. It applies based on citizenship and residency status rather than nationality alone, so temporary visa holders and companies or trusts with foreign beneficiaries can be caught by it even if they live in Australia. The surcharge is calculated on the same purchase price as the base duty and simply added to the total payable — it doesn't replace or reduce the standard bracket calculation.

faq.question: Does buying vacant land or an investment property change the calculation?
faq.answer: The underlying bracket table is usually the same regardless of whether the property is a home, an investment, or vacant land, but the concessions layered on top of it are not. First home buyer exemptions and concessions generally require you to move in and treat the property as your main residence within a set period, so an investment purchase typically pays full duty with no concession. Vacant land can qualify for a first home buyer concession in some states if you intend to build and occupy within a required timeframe, but the land-only price is usually lower than a house-and-land package, which changes which bracket it falls into — it isn't taxed at a different rate purely because it's vacant.

faq.question: When is stamp duty due, and can it be rolled into the mortgage?
faq.answer: Stamp duty is generally due at or shortly after settlement, and in most states it must be paid before the property can be transferred into your name — your conveyancer usually arranges payment as part of settlement. It can't normally be added to your home loan: lenders fund the purchase price, not the government charges around it, so duty has to come from your own savings, deposit, or other funds set aside outside the loan amount. A small number of lenders will consider capitalising it into the loan if your deposit and loan-to-value ratio leave enough headroom, but this increases both your borrowing and your interest cost over the life of the loan, so it's worth discussing with your broker or lender directly rather than assuming it's available.

sections.title: Why Stamp Duty Isn't a Flat Percentage
sections.body: Ask most buyers what stamp duty will cost and they'll quote a single percentage of the purchase price. In practice, every Australian state and territory charges transfer duty on a progressive sliding scale — the price is sliced into bands, and each band is taxed at its own rate, exactly like income tax brackets. The first tens of thousands of dollars might be taxed around 1–1.5%, the next band at 1.5–2%, and so on up to 5–7% on the portion of the price above the top threshold. Nobody pays the top rate on the whole price; they pay it only on the slice that falls above the last threshold. NSW, Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania, the ACT and the NT each set their own bands and rates, so the same property price can produce genuinely different duty bills depending on which state it's in.

sections.title: A Worked Example: $650,000 in NSW
sections.body: Take a $650,000 established home bought in NSW by a buyer who isn't a first home buyer. Using NSW's general duty bands: 1.25% applies to the first $17,000 (≈$212.50), 1.5% to the next $19,000 up to $36,000 (≈$285.00), 1.75% to the next $61,000 up to $97,000 (≈$1,067.50), 3.5% to the next $267,000 up to $364,000 (≈$9,345.00), and 4.5% to the remaining $286,000 between $364,000 and the $650,000 purchase price (≈$12,870.00). Adding every band together gives roughly $23,780 in transfer duty — close to 3.7% of the price, well below the 4.5% top band rate that applies to that final slice, because the earlier, cheaper slices were taxed at lower rates. Change the purchase price or move to a different state and the result shifts because the bands themselves are different.

sections.title: First Home Buyer Concessions and State-by-State Variation
sections.body: Most states soften the bracket calculation for eligible first home buyers, typically through a full exemption below one price threshold and a partial, tapering concession up to a higher one — NSW, Victoria and Queensland have all run schemes along these lines, each with its own caps and conditions around whether the home is new or established and whether you intend to live in it. Foreign purchasers face the opposite adjustment: an additional surcharge, generally in the 7–8% range, added on top of the standard duty in every state that levies it. Because thresholds, rates, concession caps and surcharge percentages are each set independently by state governments and revised in state budgets, the figures this calculator uses are a snapshot rather than a guarantee. Always check the current numbers with your state or territory revenue office, or have your conveyancer confirm the duty payable before you exchange contracts.
